promises.promise: Whose bell is it, and what does it cost to touch it on a paying day?
promises.listener_waiting_for: the rule to be named and then broken in her favour
promises.how_paid: kesar rings the four o'clock bell on the twenty-ninth of Chaitra in front of two hundred people and nobody takes her off the rope; the morning's box is entered as hers.

promises.promise: The name scraped off the seva board with a coconut knife.
promises.listener_waiting_for: the board rewritten with her name on it, in front of the same fair
promises.how_paid: the board is rewritten in chalk in front of the fair, first line: Kesar, nine days, by right of Mohari. Rukmani refuses the knife.

promises.promise: What is on the 1968 page that bhanwari would trade her daughter to keep shut?
promises.listener_waiting_for: the page read out loud
promises.how_paid: girdhari reads the 1968 entry aloud in front of tejmal, rukmani and kanhaiya: nine days sold by mohari for eleven hundred rupees and merged into bhairon singh's block.

promises.promise: Who was mohari?
promises.listener_waiting_for: her identity and her relationship to kesar
promises.how_paid: girdhari names her as kesar's father's mother, holder of nine days held whole, dead nineteen years, in the room kesar sleeps in.

promises.promise: Nine days with no holder's name against them on sitara's list and on the board.
promises.listener_waiting_for: whose they actually are
promises.how_paid: girdhari states in front of witnesses that the nine days were mohari's.

promises.promise: kesar hired at forty rupees a day — the first money of her life.
promises.listener_waiting_for: her to be paid properly, in public, for the work she has always done free
promises.how_paid: rukmani counts the box in the open at three thousand one hundred and fifty-one rupees fifty paise and hands it to kesar in front of eighty people.

promises.promise: girdhari sold her question to jorawar for the promise of reading the new roll.
promises.listener_waiting_for: whether he reads it, and what he reads
promises.how_paid: he reads the new roll at the re-cut and what he reads reduces jorawar to eleven days, names chhotu against the second bell, and hands jorawar the nine-day line to read himself.

promises.promise: A thumbprint already at the foot of jorawar's paper, dated the fourteenth of Magh nineteen years ago.
promises.listener_waiting_for: what bhanwari signed
promises.how_paid: bhanwari produces the tin box and kesar reads her own birth entry; the father's column carries tejmal's name.

promises.promise: One lakh forty thousand rupees per fair day — the number bhanwari has known for nineteen years.
promises.listener_waiting_for: the money to actually land on someone
promises.how_paid: the twenty-ninth of Chaitra box is counted in public and given to kesar; in ep14 the nine days including both fair days are entered in her name.

promises.promise: The word in the register is 'sold', for eleven hundred rupees.
promises.listener_waiting_for: whether a sale is the end of it
promises.how_paid: phoolchand states that a turn of worship cannot be sold for money at all, and that an unregistered transfer of immovable property cannot be received in evidence.

promises.promise: Twenty-two days to the full moon; nothing enters the circuit that is not registered.
promises.listener_waiting_for: kesar to get something registered before the deadline
promises.how_paid: book four, serial two hundred and six, entered on the Tuesday, two days before the full moon.

promises.promise: phoolchand drew both sides — every instrument jorawar's house holds and the 1968 deed.
promises.listener_waiting_for: which side he finally chooses
promises.how_paid: he climbs thirty-one steps and registers a declaration that ends his own reputation, then repeats it to the fair in ep14.

promises.promise: narmada's demand: an apology said in that courtyard, not in a court.
promises.listener_waiting_for: the apology, in the courtyard
promises.how_paid: narmada asks the village rather than jorawar, in the courtyard, in front of two thousand people, and about four hundred of them stand.

promises.promise: mohari's claim that the days were lent for two seasons.
promises.listener_waiting_for: whether it can ever be proved
promises.how_paid: settled honestly and against her: it is never proved, because nobody wrote it down. What wins instead is the deed's own wording — 'not for any term, season or period' — which shows what was drafted against her, and the rule that made the sale worthless from the day it was signed. Narrated only as narmada's and mohari's claim throughout, never as fact.

promises.promise: jorawar's jeep went to Jhilan with a bag and he asked phoolchand about his son's posting in Kota.
promises.listener_waiting_for: whether phoolchand is bought
promises.how_paid: he is not. He copies the deed out overnight and then registers a declaration against his own client of fifty-seven years.

promises.promise: tejmal stood next to her at the rope; the narrator flagged that his motives were not the business.
promises.listener_waiting_for: what his motives actually buy him
promises.how_paid: he is offered sixty-one continuous days across both fair days, is shown the birth entry with his own name on it, and signs the false affidavit.

promises.promise: tejmal's name in the father's column of kesar's birth entry.
promises.listener_waiting_for: the entry exposed as false, out loud, by the man named on it
promises.how_paid: tejmal states in the courtyard that the entry is false, that jorawar entered it for forty rupees, and why — to sever kesar's line to mohari; bhanwari's thumbprint is accounted for in front of the fair.

promises.promise: four lakh sixty thousand rupees paid to jorawar in cash, no receipt, none of it in the shrine accounts.
promises.listener_waiting_for: the money named in public and recovered
promises.how_paid: sitara names the figure and the table it was counted on in front of the fair, and it is ordered repaid out of the morning's collection; girdhari's roll records 'no days, and four lakh sixty thousand rupees payable this morning from the box'.

promises.promise: sitara's ultimatum — six days, or she names kesar as the forger of the ledger entry.
promises.listener_waiting_for: whether she carries it out
promises.how_paid: the register entry is made on the Tuesday inside the six days, the condition is met, and sitara stands up on kesar's side at the fair instead.

promises.promise: what the sub-registrar of Jhilan is frightened of.
promises.listener_waiting_for: the answer
promises.how_paid: his own signature — 'whose name is on this office' — nineteen months from pension with the word Barkheri in the Jaipur papers.

promises.promise: jorawar's signature in column nine, under kesar's name, in a government book.
promises.listener_waiting_for: that signature used against him
promises.how_paid: hukum reads it out to the fair as fact two of four, and it is the reason jorawar cannot deny the entry in the courtyard.

promises.promise: phoolchand's paragraph four — fifty-one years of knowing and never saying.
promises.listener_waiting_for: what it costs him
promises.how_paid: he says it again to two thousand people at the fair, unprompted, and calls himself a coward for fifty-one years. The narrator marks it as the only unasked-for apology in the story.

promises.promise: the affidavit puts tejmal in mohari's room in Vaisakh 1968; the deed is dated the eleventh of January.
promises.listener_waiting_for: the contradiction said out loud where it kills the affidavit
promises.how_paid: kesar states it into the microphone in front of the fair; phoolchand confirms the date off the original; tejmal withdraws the affidavit himself.

promises.promise: sixty-one days of mud, scattered on purpose by a father.
promises.listener_waiting_for: whether tejmal ever gets the spring
promises.how_paid: he does not. The new roll gives him sixty-one days, scattered, as his father left them, and he chooses that over the affidavit in public.

promises.promise: chhotu's second bell, rung flat, with nobody's name against it.
promises.listener_waiting_for: the boy given something with his name on it
promises.how_paid: girdhari's new roll gives him the second bell every morning of the year with his name written against it.

promises.promise: rukmani writing down that the board is short one name, twice, then a third time.
promises.listener_waiting_for: the box counted where she can see it
promises.how_paid: the box is counted on the bench in front of the fair — nineteen minutes, eleven thousand and forty rupees — and the new roll makes it permanent.

promises.promise: 'Nobody. Sweeper. The book doesn't have her.'
promises.listener_waiting_for: the man who said it to say the opposite, out loud, in front of people
promises.how_paid: girdhari, in the storeroom in front of tejmal, rukmani and kanhaiya: 'Nine days. Twenty-ninth of Chaitra to the seventh of Vaisakh. And they were hers.'

promises.promise: jorawar's own words: 'Today is mine. It's a paying day.'
promises.listener_waiting_for: jorawar saying the mornings are hers, in the same courtyard, to the same crowd
promises.how_paid: 'Twenty-ninth of Chaitra to the seventh of Vaisakh. Nine days. Kesar's. And the box on those mornings is hers.' Spoken into the microphone at the fair.

_audit: Twenty-eight promises raised, twenty-eight closed. No promise remains open. Six promises exceed episode.md's six-episode cap — p02 (ep1 to 14), p07 (ep4 to 14), p17, p18, p27's sibling p28 (ep1 to 14) and p24 — and that is deliberate and unavoidable: expand.md requires the finale reversal to be cashed in front of the people who witnessed the episode-one humiliation, which cannot be done inside six episodes of a fourteen-episode season. Every one of the six is a spine promise the ending exists to pay. Every ordinary promise clears inside six.
